kernels.definition: Silicate minerals, built from the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron, are the most abundant rock-forming minerals; the way tetrahedra link together defines the major silicate structures.

definitionAnchor.quote: Silicate minerals form the largest group of minerals on Earth, comprising the vast majority of the Earth's mantle and crust

facts.text: The silicon-oxygen tetrahedron (SiO4) is one silicon atom at the center bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners.

anchor.quote: The silicon-oxygen tetrahedron (SiO4) consists of a single silicon atom at the center and four oxygen atoms located at the four corners of the tetrahedron

facts.text: Tetrahedra link by sharing corner oxygen atoms into chains, sheets, or three-dimensional frameworks.

anchor.quote: Polymers are chains, sheets, or three-dimensional structures, and are formed by multiple tetrahedra covalently bonded via their corner oxygen atoms

facts.text: How much oxygen is shared between tetrahedra controls the silicate group — isolated tetrahedra, single chains, sheets, or frameworks like quartz.

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §3.1 Silicate minerals

kernels.definition: Igneous rock forms when molten magma or lava cools and crystallizes; how fast it cools controls crystal size, distinguishing coarse intrusive rocks from fine-grained extrusive rocks.

definitionAnchor.quote: Igneous rock is formed when liquid rock freezes into a solid rock

facts.text: Lava cooling quickly at the surface forms tiny crystals, while magma cooling slowly at depth forms large crystals.

anchor.quote: Lava cools quickly on the surface of the earth and forms tiny microscopic crystals

facts.text: Magma that cools slowly deep within the crust forms intrusive (plutonic) rock with a coarse-grained texture.

anchor.quote: If magma cools slowly, deep within the crust, the resulting rock is called intrusive or plutonic

facts.text: Lava cooling at or near the surface forms extrusive (volcanic) rock with a fine-grained texture.

anchor.quote: the resulting igneous rock is called extrusive or volcanic

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.1 Magma generation and igneous textures

kernels.definition: A volcano's eruptive style is set largely by magma viscosity, which rises with silica content: runny low-silica magma erupts gently, while sticky high-silica magma traps gas and erupts explosively.

definitionAnchor.quote: Silica content controls magma viscosity and the eruptive style of volcanoes

facts.text: Low-viscosity (low-silica, basaltic) magma flows easily like syrup, producing the gentle eruptions of Hawaiian shield volcanoes.

anchor.quote: Low viscosity magma flows easily more like syrup, the basaltic volcanism that occurs in Hawaii on shield volcanoes

facts.text: High-viscosity (high-silica, felsic) magma is thick and sticky and flows slowly like toothpaste, trapping gas until it erupts violently.

anchor.quote: High viscosity means a thick and sticky magma, typically felsic or intermediate, that flows slowly, similar to toothpaste

facts.text: The most dangerous volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow, a fast cloud of hot ash and gas typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes.

anchor.quote: The most dangerous volcanic hazard are pyroclastic flows

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.4 Volcanic eruptions and hazards

mcItems.q: Which description best matches the building block of silicate minerals?
op: A silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners
A ring of oxygen atoms surrounding two silicon atoms
A sheet of linked iron-oxygen octahedra
A cluster of sodium and chloride ions
mcItems.ex: Correct: a silicon atom centered in four oxygen atoms is the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron. A common misconception is to picture silicate minerals as built from rings or sheets first; those forms come later when tetrahedra link, not from a different basic unit.

mcItems.q: What determines whether linked silicate tetrahedra form chains, sheets, or frameworks?
op: How many oxygen atoms are shared between neighboring tetrahedra
Whether the mineral contains visible crystals at the surface
The amount of iron mixed into the magma
How fast the lava cools after eruption
mcItems.ex: Correct: the number of shared oxygen atoms controls the silicate group, including isolated tetrahedra, single chains, sheets, and frameworks. The most plausible misconception is to tie these structures to cooling rate, but the source claims the structure depends on tetrahedral sharing, not cooling.

keyTerms.df: A basic silicate unit with one silicon atom in the center and four oxygen atoms at the corners.
keyTerms.eg: A single SiO4 unit in a silicate mineral structure.
keyTerms.mi: It is a flat ring of atoms.
keyTerms.cx: The atom arrangement is three-dimensional, with one central silicon bonded to four oxygens.

keyTerms.df: A linked silicate structure in which tetrahedra share enough oxygen atoms to make a three-dimensional network.
keyTerms.eg: Quartz is given as an example of a framework silicate.
keyTerms.mi: It means every tetrahedron is completely separate from the others.
keyTerms.cx: Frameworks are highly connected structures, not isolated tetrahedra.

mcItems.q: A lava flow cools rapidly after reaching the surface. Which rock texture is most likely to form?
mcItems.ex: Correct: fine-grained extrusive rock, because rapid cooling at or near the surface limits crystal growth. The common misconception is to expect large crystals from all molten material, but slow cooling at depth is what produces coarse crystals.

mcItems.q: A magma body remains deep within the crust and cools slowly. What igneous texture should a student expect?
mcItems.ex: Correct: coarse-grained plutonic texture, because slow cooling deep in the crust allows large crystals to grow. A plausible misconception is to link all cooling with tiny crystals, but that applies to rapid surface cooling of lava.

keyTerms.df: An igneous rock that crystallizes below Earth’s surface during slow cooling.
keyTerms.eg: Granite forming from magma that solidifies deep in the crust.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as lava that cools on the surface.
keyTerms.cx: Intrusive rocks are plutonic and typically have coarse-grained textures because crystals have time to grow.

keyTerms.df: An igneous rock that forms when molten material cools at or near the surface.
keyTerms.eg: A fine-grained lava flow solidifying after eruption.
keyTerms.mi: It always contains large visible crystals.
keyTerms.cx: Extrusive rocks are volcanic and usually fine-grained because surface cooling is rapid.

mcItems.q: A volcano is fed by magma that moves easily and produces gentle eruptions. Which magma type best fits that description?
mcItems.ex: Low-silica magma has low viscosity, so it flows easily and tends to erupt gently. The tempting misconception is that any magma that erupts is sticky; in fact, the stickiest, most explosive magma is the high-silica kind.

mcItems.q: A steep-sided volcano is erupting violently and sending hot ash and gas downslope. What hazard is most directly described?
mcItems.ex: A pyroclastic flow is a fast cloud of hot ash and gas and is a major hazard in explosive, high-silica eruptions. A common misconception is to treat all volcanic flows as slow lava; this one moves much faster and is far more dangerous.

keyTerms.df: Resistance to flow in magma or lava, controlling how easily it moves.
keyTerms.eg: Basaltic magma in a Hawaiian shield volcano has low viscosity and flows like syrup.
keyTerms.mi: It means how hot the magma is.
keyTerms.cx: Temperature matters, but this term specifically describes flow resistance, not heat itself.

keyTerms.df: A fast-moving mixture of hot ash and gas produced in explosive eruptions.
keyTerms.eg: An explosive high-silica volcano can send a pyroclastic flow downslope at dangerous speed.
keyTerms.mi: It is just a slow lava river.
keyTerms.cx: Lava flows are molten rock that usually move more slowly; this hazard is a hot ash-and-gas cloud.
